notes.title: How the cuisine filters were policed
notes.body: Vietnamese — only Vietnamese-owned or Vietnamese-family kitchens named by local press. Singaporean — the menu had to carry actual Singaporean dishes; “Singapore noodles” would have disqualified a place, and Cleveland has exactly one that passes. Chinese — the regional tradition is stated on each card (Cantonese, Sichuan) and only places raved about by Cleveland Scene, Cleveland Magazine or Freshwater are here. Unique American, European, Latin American — had to be viral or heavily raved, no generic burger or pizza. Middle Eastern — you asked specifically about Persian; there is no Persian restaurant in Cleveland with that reputation, so I have said so on the card rather than padding the list. Two Bourdain restaurants are included even though they are permanently closed, so you know they are gone rather than hunting for them.

notes.title: What the web turned up
notes.body: Most Cleveland "hidden gems" listicles online are recycled SEO with no local reporting, so I did not use them. The one genuinely useful find was that Atlas Obscura catalogues around 33 Cleveland places — your four links were a fraction of it — so the rest are now included and tagged ATLAS OBSCURA. Everything tagged ADDED is from my own knowledge rather than a specific article: places locals treat as essential that the hidden-gem lists skip precisely because they are not hidden.

places.w: Civil War memorial with a free museum inside — bronze reliefs, marble busts, knowledgeable volunteers. Beneath it runs a labyrinth of tunnels that opens to the public one day a year.
places.k: Ask at the desk whether a tunnel tour is scheduled. Interior alone: 20–30 minutes. Free.

places.n: Chess Collection — Cleveland Public Library MAIN Library
places.ad: 325 Superior Ave NE · Main Building, 3rd floor, John G. White Special Collections
places.w:
This is the right building. The 1925 Main Library on Superior Avenue — not a branch, not the Louis Stokes Wing next door. Go in the Main Building, take the marble staircase to the third floor, and pass through the John Griswold White Exhibition Corridor (look for owls in the wrought-iron cases) into Special Collections.

Inside is the John G. White Chess and Checkers Collection: the largest chess collection in the world. Over 35,000 items going back to the 12th century — one-of-a-kind sets from every continent, rare manuscripts, Bobby Fischer score sheets, Lasker medals, the most comprehensive tournament records anywhere, and two death masks of Gisela Kahn Gresser, nine-time US women's champion. White was a Cleveland attorney who collected from 1870 until his death in 1928, buying up entire European and American chess libraries; the library has kept collecting since. It has been on this floor since the doors opened.
places.k:
Bring photo ID such as a driving licence. It is a closed research collection — you request items and are shown one at a time, so email special.collections@cpl.org ahead if you want something specific pulled. Closed Sunday.

Note: News 5's list prints the address as 525 Superior. That is wrong — the Main Library is at 325 Superior Ave.

places.w: Five-story glass-roofed atrium built in 1890 as America's first indoor shopping centre, modelled on Milan's Galleria and financed in part by Rockefeller. Top three floors are now a Hyatt. A Superman film was shot here.
places.k: Stand at the far end and look up the full height. Grab Pizza 216 while you're in.

places.w: Two smaller arcades running alongside each other, less grand than the Old Arcade but full of independent shops and cafés. One near 5th Street sells assorted knick-knacks and candy.
The 42nd floor of a 52-story tower that was briefly the world's second-tallest. Views across the bridges, the Cuyahoga and Lake Erie. Small and dated in a way that's part of the appeal.
places.k: Book online in advance — no walk-ups. Check in at the ground-floor desk, ride to 32, transfer to 42. Around $5–6. Weekends only.

places.w: The oldest building on Public Square. You have driven past it a hundred times and never gone in — the stained glass and the all-wood arched ceiling are the reason to.
places.k: Interior access is inconsistent. Try during a service or a scheduled tour.

places.ad: Rockwell Ave, between the library buildings
places.w: A walled garden of public art and trees wedged between the two library buildings — the quietest square of downtown. Jazz concerts on summer Wednesdays.
A grocery store inside the old Cleveland Trust Company bank rotunda — stained-glass dome, marble, murals. Go up to the balcony seating and eat lunch under it.

pv.ss: Signal Cleveland and TheStreet: Heinen's permanently closed its downtown store (900 Euclid, Cleveland Trust rotunda) on July 31, 2026

places.w: Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen's giant rubber stamp, tipped on its side, reading FREE. Roughly 28 × 26 × 49 feet. Commissioned for a corporate plaza, rejected, then exiled here — arguably the better ending.
A pocket-sized Liberty on a downtown sidewalk. Considerably easier to reach on a Saturday afternoon than the original.
A restored 1875 warehouse block in the Warehouse District with a genuinely delightful interior atrium. Blue Point Grille is downstairs.
A surprising patch of downtown green that somehow escaped becoming an eyesore parking lot, with views out to Lake Erie and several statues scattered through it.

places.ad: Fort Huntington Park, 299 W Lakeside Ave
places.w: William McVey's 1982 bronze. Owens was born in Alabama and died in Arizona, but he spent his formative years in Cleveland before winning four golds at the 1936 Berlin Olympics — in front of a regime whose entire racial theory he demolished in a week.

places.ad: 300 Lakeside Ave, front of the centre by the RAPID tracks
places.w: A working micro-farm in the middle of downtown, right beside the rail tracks. Unexpected, and we could stand to have more of it.
The last fully intact WWII fleet submarine in existence. No cut-away hull, no visitor stairs — you go in the way the crew did. Veterans narrate in person; push-button stations cover the rest.
places.k: Entry is down a vertical ladder through a deck hatch. Not accessible, and genuinely tight. Seasonal — confirm before driving out.

places.w: Pei's glass pyramid on the lakefront, five floors of exhibits. Even if you're not a devotee the history of how the music got made — and the DJs who took the risks — carries it.
places.k: Buy ahead. Budget three hours minimum; six if you're thorough.

places.n: Voinovich Bicentennial Park & Cleveland Lighthouse view
places.w: Behind the Rock Hall. Walk to the water and the Cleveland Lighthouse is visible offshore — in hard winters it ices over into a frozen tower. One of the Cleveland script signs is here.

places.ad: North Coast Harbor, E 9th Street Pier (and five others)
places.w: The city script signs are scattered around Cleveland and each frames a different view. All six: North Coast Harbor (E 9th Street Pier, by the Rock Hall) · Tremont (1502 Abbey Ave, best downtown view) · Edgewater Park (6500 Cleveland Memorial Shoreway) · Euclid Beach (16301 Lakeshore Blvd) · The Foundry (1831 Columbus Rd) · Cleveland Hopkins Airport (near baggage claim).
places.k: The Tremont and Edgewater signs are the two worth going out of your way for — Tremont for the skyline, Edgewater for the sunset.

places.w: Cleveland's largest sightseeing ship, up the Cuyahoga through the Flats and out onto Lake Erie. It drew more reader nominations than anything else on the hidden-gems list.

places.n: Azure Rooftop Lounge at The 9 — CLOSED
places.w: Twelve floors up, open air, skyline in every direction. Nothing hot on the menu — come for the view and a cold drink.

pv.ss: Yelp lists 'Azure Rooftop Lounge - CLOSED' (updated May 2026); the 2017 E 9th rooftop at The Metropolitan at The 9 was replaced by The Garden of Eden rooftop

places.w: In-house brewery, butcher and charcutier on pedestrianised East 4th. Shared plates. Order the baked pretzel and ask for the roasted garlic caramel sauce — it sounds wrong and isn't.

places.n: Greater Cleveland Aquarium — shark gallery & seatube
places.w: Built inside the old FirstEnergy powerhouse in the Flats. The seatube walks you beside, around and under three shark species.
Beneath the road deck sits an abandoned streetcar level — tunnels, tiled walls and four original subway tracks, standing as they did in 1917.
places.k: Opens for public tours roughly once a year, usually in June. Free. Watch for the announcement; it's worth planning a trip around.

places.ad: Washington Ave & Center St, The Flats
places.w: Scale replicas of the Hope Memorial Bridge pylon figures, at street level in the Flats. Almost nobody knows they exist.

places.ad: Beside 1148 Main Ave, at the jackknife bridge
places.w: A Norse explorer glowering out of Cleveland's smallest park, at the foot of the Cuyahoga jackknife bridge. The Scandinavian community gathers here once a year for a toast on Leif Erikson Day.
A mural where Cleveland's history and the cosmos intersect, on the Columbus Road approach into the Flats.
A rowing and sailing centre in a converted industrial building on the river, open to the public for programmes. Skyline and freighter views from the dock. A Cleveland script sign sits outside.
A pedal-powered bar-boat on the Cuyahoga. The least sober and most enjoyable way to see the river.
Lakefront park on Whiskey Island with volleyball courts, a lighthouse view and trails connecting to Edgewater. Every September monarchs arriving from Canada stop here en masse on the way to Mexico.
places.k: The migration window is short. Watch Cleveland Metroparks for the announcement.

places.w: Hole-in-the-wall turning out Hong Kong-style bubble waffles and milk tea. Closed Tuesdays. Large lot outside.
An art gallery and small live-music room hidden in a warehouse by Asia Town. Underground, punk-adjacent, genuinely good.
places.k: Thursday to Sunday only.

places.w: An artist collective of 60–80 members in the half-abandoned, beautiful Hamilton building — home to IngenuityFest and Brite Winter. Anyone can volunteer to build exhibits.
A community garden for motorcycle repair — shared tools, shared knowledge — that also has a bar and live music. Members bring in salvage bikes and rebuild them with help.

pv.ss: News 5 Cleveland: 'Skidmark Garage is closing after 11 years'; closed April 30, 2026 due to financial difficulties/bankruptcy

places.n: Percy Skuy Collection, Dittrick Medical History Center
places.ad: 11000 Euclid Ave, Allen Memorial Medical Library
places.w: The largest and most comprehensive collection of historical contraceptives in the world — over a thousand objects arranged chronologically across a millennium. Beaver testicles, crocodile dung, mule earwax, spider carcasses, Mexican yams, Goodyear rubbers, IUDs. Alongside sit the texts: Casanova recommending a hollowed half-lemon, and 1580 BCE instructions involving ground dates, acacia and honey. The wider Dittrick galleries on medical history are excellent in their own right.
places.k: Very limited hours and they should drive your whole day. Free. Metered street parking.

places.w: Formally "The Angel of Death Victorious." A life-size bronze on the Haserot family plot, holding an extinguished torch upside down. Decades of oxidation have left black streaks running from her eyes down her neck, so she appears to weep. Herman Matzen sculpted her; canning magnate Francis Haserot commissioned her after his wife died in 1919.
places.k: Easy to miss — just off the road under trees. Grab a map at the gate; nearest marked landmark is the Hanna Mausoleum.

places.w: 280 acres, 100,000 graves, and the best architecture walk in the city: the James A. Garfield Memorial and tomb, Wade Memorial Chapel with a Louis Tiffany interior, and mausoleums throughout. Climb the Garfield tower for a downtown view.
places.k: Maps at the gate, main office and Garfield Monument. Bikes allowed. A trolley tour runs at 1pm — call to book. Open every day of the year.

places.w: A working dam inside the cemetery grounds, built to hold back Dugway Brook and supply the city. Most visitors never find it.
A jukebox headstone for the Cleveland disc jockey credited with coining the phrase rock and roll.

One of the largest museums in the country, free to enter. The 1916 building, East and West wings and North building wrap a glass-roofed atrium. Armour court, Egyptian galleries, strong Asian collection upstairs in the North building.
places.k: Enter via Wade Park and the South entrance for the approach across the lagoon. Special exhibitions are ticketed; the permanent collection isn't. Closed Monday.

places.w: The formal garden and lagoon in front of the art museum. Olmsted Jr. called it a development placed exactly where the greatest number of people would pass it daily. Harpists, wedding parties, and a lot of geese.

places.n: Lucy, at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History
places.w: The Australopithecus afarensis skeleton — the oldest discovered link in the chain of human evolution, and Cleveland's most famous resident. Balto the sled dog is here too, taxidermied and on display. Live animals outside, including a bald eagle.
places.k: Planetarium and 3D films cost extra. Attached garage. Two hours minimum. Closed Monday.

places.ad: Cleveland Museum of Natural History, 1 Wade Oval Dr
places.w: A chunk of the moon collected by Alan Bean on 20 November 1969, on long-term loan from NASA. There is nothing else like it on earth, which is the entire point.

places.ad: East Blvd at Euclid Ave, University Circle
places.w: The park wrapped around the lagoon, between MOCA and the art museum. Walk the far side of the water for the classic view of the Cleveland Museum of Art reflected across it.
Glasshouses of Costa Rican cloud forest and Madagascan spiny desert, a butterfly house, plus outdoor Japanese, herb and rose gardens. Closed Monday.
Farshid Moussavi's black faceted geometric building — worth seeing from outside alone. Three of four floors are exhibition space; the fourth is working artists. Free for Ohio residents.
places.k: Thursday to Sunday only.

places.n: Cleveland History Center & Euclid Beach Carousel
places.w: The restored 1910 Euclid Beach Park carousel, which you can ride, inside a museum that also holds a very large collection of historic cars and a historic house.
places.k: Odd opening days — Thursday to Sunday. Check before going.

places.ad: Martin Luther King Jr Dr, Cleveland Cultural Gardens
places.w: Modelled on the Chinese Imperial Palace and dedicated in 1985. Two guardian lions flank the entrance — one with a ball beneath his paw, one with a cub — and Confucius stands on a white pedestal. The only cultural garden east of E 105th.

A city-owned greenhouse from 1905 grown into a full botanical facility: globally themed gardens, native Ohio plants, a tropical house. The cactus and desert room is the one people remember. Free, and rarely crowded.
places.k: Closes at 4pm, earlier than everything around it. Free parking; iris garden across the lot.

places.w: The oldest and only surviving pre-Civil War structure in University Circle, now an interpretive centre on Cleveland's role in the Underground Railroad and the local abolitionist movement.
places.k: Saturday afternoons only.

places.w: Cleveland's shortest street at 300 feet — and it's paved with wooden blocks. There is nowhere else like it in the city.
Curated vintage clothing, jewellery and oddments in Little Italy, run by an owner who clearly enjoys it. Prices are unusually fair.
places.k: Thursday to Sunday. Pair with a Little Italy meal or food tour.

places.w: Vacant lots in the Hough neighbourhood turned into a working vineyard and winery — founded by Mansfield Frazier partly as a re-entry employment project. Private tastings; walk the vines.
places.k: Wednesday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.

places.n: Baseball Heritage Museum at League Park
places.w: A free museum on the site of League Park, where Babe Ruth and Shoeless Joe Jackson played and where a replica field still stands. Small, and the guides are exceptional.
A gallery exclusively featuring artists of colour, in the Fairfax neighbourhood — the same area as Karamu House, where Langston Hughes developed his plays.
places.k: Friday to Sunday afternoons only.

places.w: Older than Lake View and far less visited. Graves of people born only years after independence, veterans of 1812 and the Civil War, and a deep vein of Black Cleveland history that volunteers are still recovering.
Less a museum than a play space, inside a Millionaires' Row mansion. Closed Thursdays; mornings only.
James Simon's 18-foot trumpeter and his dog, permanent greeters at the Buckeye Jazz Festival.
An enigmatic marked doorway off Chester Avenue that a certain kind of person insists is a gateway to an alternate universe. Limited appeal, too odd to leave out.
A man turned his house and lawn into a personal art collective. Eclectic, messy, wonderfully weird. View respectfully from the pavement — this is somebody's home.
Tim Willis turns scrap into larger-than-life trucks and robots on his own lot. Another one to view from the street.

places.ad: E 49th St, just north of Fleet Ave
places.w: A rails-to-trails success story linking Slavic Village to Garfield Park Reservation and the county's tallest waterfall.
An 1891 Polish Gothic church with hand-carved wooden altar statues, a pipe organ, painted cathedral ceiling and two first-class relics including one of John Paul II. Genuinely jaw-dropping.

places.ad: Lee Road Library, 2345 Lee Rd, Cleveland Heights
places.w: A bronze desk-and-figure tribute to the American Splendor author, at the library that was one of his haunts.

Go to the back door of the barbershop and spa. Press the buzzer. Say you're there to see a man about a horse. Up the stairs, turn right, find the bookshelf, pull the correct book — the wall opens onto a 1920s bar.
places.k: Closed Sunday and Monday. Small capacity; the attic room is the quiet one. They run cocktail classes.

places.ad: North Park Blvd near Woodmere Dr, Shaker Heights
places.w: A row of Liberty Oaks planted as living memorials to soldiers killed in the First World War. A century on, a number still stand.
Seasonal, and non-negotiable if you're here in December. It isn't Christmas in Cleveland without it.
places.k: Late November through early January only.

pv.ss: Cleveland Scene: 'Nela Park's Christmas Light Display Goes Dark After 100 Years With No Festivities for 2025 Season' + News5

places.w: A capped landfill turned birding reserve, with a 1.5-mile flat perimeter trail and views of the skyline, Bratenahl and the lake. You have driven past it on I-90 a hundred times.

A hundred stalls under a 1912 barrel-vaulted hall with a clock tower — butchers, bakers, fishmongers, cheesemongers, spice sellers. Kielbasa in every form: smoked, fresh, double-smoked, Hungarian, Polish. One stand is called the Pork Chop Shop. Food has been sold on or beside this site since 1840. Look for the steer's head carved into the northern pediment, and go up to the balcony for the view down the hall.
places.k: Bring cash — most stalls don't take cards. First hour of parking free; park toward the back near the beer garden. The outdoor produce arcade is a separate building and a harder sell than the main hall. Closed Tuesday and Thursday.

places.n: Great Lakes Brewing Co. — the bullet holes
places.w: Ohio's first craft brewery, across from the market. There are bullet holes in the mahogany bar; the story says they were either meant for Eliot Ness or fired by him.

Raymond Buckland — leader of what became the Long Island Coven — started this collection in a Bay Shore basement in the 1960s. It followed him to New Hampshire, through legal disputes in New Orleans, into storage in Columbus, and finally here. Much of it originally belonged to Gerald Gardner, father of Gardnerian Wicca, including his besom. Also: Sybil Leek's crystal ball, Egyptian ushabtis, a carved mandrake root, Crowley material, rare Ouija memorabilia, and a demon in a box that Buckland captured in the 1970s with help from a ceremonial magician.
places.k: Ten minutes from downtown. Parking behind the building and on the street. Photos without flash; the curator asks for no video. Small enough for an hour, dense enough to want longer.

places.w: The actual exterior house from the 1983 film, restored inside to match the movie, plus a museum of original props and costumes across the street. The tour covers why it was shot in Cleveland at all.
places.k: House interior is tour-only; tickets at the gift shop, departures every 30 minutes from 10:15am. Budget two hours. You can rent the house and sleep in Ralphie's bedroom.

places.w: Onion domes over Tremont, and the church from The Deer Hunter. Icons, stained glass, permanent incense. If you see only one of Tremont's churches, this is it.
places.k: Weekday mornings and around services. Tremont is dense with immigrant-built churches — walk the neighbourhood for the rest.

places.w: Build-your-own tacos with Day of the Dead murals by local artist Mac in every location. Busy on game nights; takeaway is easy.

places.ad: Professor Ave, Starkweather to W 10th St
places.w: Tremont's restaurants set up stalls the length of Professor Avenue. Held the third Sunday of July. Go around 6pm when it thins out.
places.k: One day a year. If you've missed it: Grumpy's Cafe, Lucky's Cafe, Hi and Dry, the South Side, or Tandul for Indian.

places.n: Tremont skyline view & Abbey Ave script sign
places.w: Ten minutes' walk from Professor Avenue and the best free downtown view on the west side. Best after dark when the bridge lights come up. One of the Cleveland script signs stands here.
Constructed earth mounds beside the towpath, made from Cleveland's own industrial fill, framing sweeping views of the city. A gem inside a gem.

places.ad: Multiple access points; Tremont trailhead nearest downtown
places.w: Eighty-seven miles and four counties, from Lake Erie down the old Ohio & Erie canal corridor to New Philadelphia.
A proper mural for one of the great American pizza cities, on a corner of Hingetown.
Where museums from around the world send paintings, frames and textiles to be saved. Conservators here hold degrees in both art and chemistry. A forgotten space dedicated to forgotten things.
places.k: A working lab, not a museum. Weekdays, and best approached by appointment.

places.w: John Heisman's Cleveland house — with the plaque now, finally, in front of the correct one.

places.ad: Michael Zone Recreation Center, W 53rd St
places.w: Two miles of new paved trail connecting eight Cleveland neighbourhoods along the RTA Red Line. The Cleveland people had been asking for.
Flat entry fee, unlimited play, well-kept machines, a bar. Exactly what it sounds like, which is the point.
places.k: Closed Tuesday. From 4pm weekdays, noon at weekends.

places.w: A stonemason's fever dream of a pub with an Italian bocce court inside, making a serious attempt at being the most Cleveland place in Cleveland.
A dense concentration of murals across the arts district — there's a published map so you can plan a route. Sweet Moses for ice cream when you're done.
Swimming beach, fishing pier, open yoga classes on the lawn, and a Cleveland script sign. Sunsets here are the reason locals come.
Nobody knows who planted it. It's the most famous tree in Cleveland and it has earned the title.
A 1952 amusement park whose rides have barely changed in seventy years, scaled for children eight and under. Free entry and parking, tickets never expire, and nobody tries to sell you anything.
The longest indoor mountain bike trail in the world, in a warehouse that looks abandoned from the street. Beginner floor-painted lines up to expert jump lines, a foam pit, and rental bikes.
places.k: Seasonal and limited hours — check before you load the car.

places.w: A candy warehouse, not a candy store — aisles of it, in bulk, plus an ice cream and soda counter. Went viral in 2021 for sheer volume. Prices are roughly retail; come for the spectacle.
Directly between Dang Good and Birdietown: a large playground with a genuinely tall climbing structure, tennis courts, ball fields and a summer pool. Somewhere to walk off dinner.
places.k: The pool is Lakewood residents only unless you're signed in as a guest, and it closes early — around 5:15pm.

places.w: Not the chess one — but an exceptional building in its own right, with soaring ceilings, floods of natural light, and a basement book sale that regularly turns up things you cannot find elsewhere. Open seven days.

places.n: The Sanctuary Museum (Museum of Divine Statues)
places.w: Makeup artist Lou McClung spent years rescuing statues, stained glass, altarpieces and relics from Catholic parishes across the Diocese of Cleveland as they closed, then restoring them. The result is a room of hundreds of saved objects that would otherwise have been landfilled. The wall of relics is the centrepiece — step too close and you trip the laser.
places.k: The hardest schedule on this list: two short windows a week. Small admission. Call ahead.

places.w: Terraced stone steps down to Lake Erie, built so everyone gets a front-row seat rather than a handful of benches. Best sunset in the region, with the skyline visible east. Porch swings on the bluff.
places.k: Arrive 30 minutes before sunset for a seat on the lower terraces. Windy and cold well into spring.

places.w: A small bluff-top park with steps down to the shoreline, a playground and clean facilities. Worth crossing town for even if you live east.

places.ad: Boston Mill Visitor Center, 6947 Riverview Rd, Peninsula
places.w: A full national park half an hour from downtown that a surprising number of Ohioans have never visited. Start at Boston Mill for maps and rangers.
places.k: With one afternoon and a car: Brandywine Falls, then sunset from the Ledges Overlook.

places.w: A 65-foot waterfall reached by a boardwalk from the car park, viewable from above or from the gorge floor. Different in every season.
places.k: Stairs at both viewing levels — not fully accessible. Gets very busy; go early.

places.w: Sandstone ledges, mossy crevices and a west-facing overlook that is the best sunset in the national park. Mysterious carvings are scattered through the rock.

places.ad: 2844 River Rd, North Chagrin Reservation, Willoughby Hills
places.w: A roofless stone gatehouse — all that was ever built of Feargus Squire's country estate — standing free and open on a wide lawn. Hollow inside, thick with urban myth, and beautiful in fog.
Faces and iconography carved into sandstone ledges in the 1940s by Noble Stuart, who did it in the woods his late wife had inherited. George Washington, Jefferson, a sphinx, and Ty Cobb.
places.k: Trail is marked with a raccoon-head blaze and crossed by bridle trails — easy to end up on the wrong one.

places.w: Rock ledges, small caves and free-climbing scrambles — closer than Hocking Hills and far less crowded. Swim at the spillway after.
places.k: Steeper and rockier than it looks; trails are poorly marked on the way down.

places.w: A blacksmith and self-taught artist carved Native American imagery into this riverside boulder in 1885, working at night by lantern.
The tallest waterfall in Cuyahoga County at 48 feet. Its power drove the mills that helped build the city.
A short walk down into the valley gets you Tinker's Creek Falls, mill ruins, wildflowers, trains and observation platforms — a lot packed into a small park.

places.ad: West Creek Reservation, 1969 W Ridgewood Dr, Parma
places.w: The downtown skyline seen from the suburbs — about fifteen minutes up a well-kept trail from the car park.
Stebbins Gulch is Holden's crown jewel — a ravine of cascades and waterfalls reachable only on a guided tour. The wider arboretum has a canopy walk and an emergent tower.
places.k: Gulch access is guided only and must be booked. Closed Mondays.

places.w: An 1,100-acre certified dark-sky park with a Nassau telescope programme, a scale-model solar system, a pyramid and a stone circle. Come for a meteor shower.
Sixteen acres of rare plants in a cottage-style landscape, half-returned to nature for want of hands. An unexpected green island in a stretch of retail.
places.k: Small admission. Closed Mondays.

places.w: A sprawling garden of fibreglass animals hiding behind an HVAC company's car park. Overgrown and in need of paint, which honestly improves it. Free.
The largest fully accessible playground in Northeast Ohio, built as a village of small buildings and inspired by a boy born with Spinal Muscular Atrophy.
Free, in Euclid's historic old city hall, and a room full of accordions. Frankie Yankovic, Johnny Pecon, and the Slovenian roots of Cleveland-style polka. The Softball Hall of Fame is next door.
places.k: Wednesday and Saturday mornings only.

places.w: Edgewater isn't the only lakefront park in the county. A mansion, a beach cove, a fishing pier and a new jogging path, with far fewer people.
A clifftop park with swings, picnic tables and an underrated sunset. Pack something from Alesci's at Shoregate on the way.
Sixty-nine steps to a walkway around the lantern and a view over the harbour, plus a Great Lakes shipping museum below. Ask about the ghost cat.
places.k: Wednesday, Friday, weekends. Around $10.

places.ad: King Memorial Rd, north of Little Mountain Rd, Kirtland Hills
places.w: An optical illusion of terrain: the road appears to run uphill, and a car in neutral rolls the way it shouldn't.
Seventy years of popcorn, ice cream and unclassifiable sweets in a tiny shop that sits directly above the falls the village is named for.
An orchard on a ridge above the valley. Go for a sunset concert; in autumn it becomes a full festival with a super slide and corn mazes.
places.k: Heavily seasonal — much of the year it's events-only.

places.n: Cleveland Orchestra at Blossom Music Center
places.ad: 1145 W Steels Corners Rd, Cuyahoga Falls
places.w: One of the world's great orchestras, outdoors on a wooded hillside, every summer. Lawn tickets are cheap and the acoustics carry.
places.k: Summer season only. Traffic leaving the car parks is a known ordeal.

places.w: The Black River drops through a gorge in the middle of Elyria and West Falls is the headline — one of the best waterfalls in Ohio. Paved path to the falls if the trails are too steep, plus rock formations along the river.
The other set of falls in Elyria, with a boardwalk right along the water. News 5's entire write-up was: look at it. LOOK. AT. IT.

places.ad: Corner of Main & Lorain Streets, Oberlin
places.w: One of only about twenty benches worldwide placed by the Toni Morrison Society to mark the lives of enslaved Africans — a response to Morrison's remark that there was no memorial bench by the road. Morrison was born in nearby Lorain.
A large painted veterans' memorial wall, and there is more to it than the photographs show.

The Hannes Tiedemann house, 1881 — a Victorian sandstone pile with a history of family deaths and a reputation as the most haunted house in Ohio. Atlas Obscura has its own entry for it; your four links were only a fraction of what they list for Cleveland.
places.k: Interior access is by booked tour or overnight stay only, currently Tuesday evenings. The exterior and the surrounding Franklin Boulevard mansions are free to walk.

places.w: From outside, an unremarkable cemetery chapel. Inside, a Louis Tiffany interior: a monumental stained-glass window and glass mosaic murals running the length of both walls, executed by an all-female workshop. It was the first place in Cleveland outside a private home to have electric light. The bronze doors weigh two tons and swing on a finger.
places.k: Open daily 10–4, free, and there is usually a volunteer docent inside who will tell you far more than any placard. Do this in the same visit as the Haserot Angel and Garfield's tomb.

places.ad: Cleveland Museum of Art, 11150 East Blvd
places.w: A Rodin cast at the museum's south entrance, and one of very few in the world deliberately left damaged. A bomb detonated at its base in 1970 — attributed to the Weather Underground — tore off the lower legs and pedestal. The museum chose not to restore it.

places.ad: Cleveland Museum of Natural History, 1 Wade Oval Dr
places.w: The sled dog who led the final leg of the 1925 serum run to Nome, taxidermied and on display in Cleveland since 1927 — the city bought him out of a Los Angeles dime museum by public subscription.

The largest outdoor chandelier in North America, hung 44 feet above Euclid Avenue: 4,200 crystals, each placed by hand at roughly twenty minutes apiece. It anchors Playhouse Square, the largest performing arts centre in the United States outside Lincoln Center — five restored 1920s theatres saved from demolition by a volunteer campaign.
places.k: Free and lit every night. Go after dark. Parking nearby is genuinely difficult.

places.w: A 618-foot Great Lakes freighter tied up beside the Science Center, open stem to stern — engine room, pilot house, crew quarters and the panelled guest staterooms. The deck gives one of the better skyline views in the city.
places.k: Closed Monday, and seasonal. Included with Great Lakes Science Center membership.

places.ad: Burke Lakefront Airport, 1501 N Marginal Rd
places.w: Free, open during airport hours, and almost entirely overlooked — the concourse of a working lakefront airport turned into a museum of women in aviation and spaceflight.

places.n: Hope Memorial Bridge & the Guardians of Traffic
places.ad: Hope Memorial Bridge, over the Cuyahoga
places.w: Eight art deco sandstone giants, each 43 feet tall, holding vehicles from a hay wagon to a 1930s truck — Henry Hering's Guardians of Traffic, carved into the bridge pylons in 1932. The baseball team took its name from them. Pedestrian walkways run both sides.
places.k: Walk it rather than drive it. Best light is late afternoon from the west end.

places.ad: Peninsula Depot, 1630 Mill St W, Peninsula
places.w: A heritage train through the national park, run largely by volunteer conductors who narrate as you go. There is a dome car. You can also put a bike on board, ride one way and cycle the towpath back.
places.k: Book ahead — peak-season and autumn-colour runs sell out.

places.w: A Croatian social hall in North Collinwood turned into the club that broke half the bands you like before anyone else would book them. Two rooms — the small Tavern and the Ballroom — plus a record and vintage shop in the basement. The anchor of the Waterloo Arts District.
places.k: Check the calendar before making the trip; it's a fair way out. Sunday brunch is a local institution.

places.w: The largest art and design complex in Northeast Ohio — a 170,000 sq ft former Baker Electric car factory now holding dozens of galleries, studios, and two small theatres. On Third Fridays the whole building opens up.
places.k: Third Friday is the night to come and needs two to three hours. Otherwise open daytimes, closed Sunday.

places.w: A 1924 electrical substation converted into a contemporary art gallery, run jointly with the Cleveland Museum of Art. Free, small, and consistently more interesting than its size suggests. Rotating exhibitions only, so there is always something new.
places.k: Thursday to Sunday. Combine with an Ohio City brewery walk.

places.w: Home of the Cleveland Orchestra — by most reckonings one of the finest orchestras in the world — in a 1931 hall whose art deco and Egyptian Revival interior is worth the ticket on its own.
places.k: Season runs roughly September to May; in summer the orchestra decamps to Blossom. Metered street parking is often free in the evening — check ParkMobile before paying $20 to the garage.

places.w: The oldest Black theatre in the United States, founded 1915. Langston Hughes developed his plays here. Recently renovated and still producing.

The oldest building in Cleveland still standing on its original site — an 1824 stagecoach tavern on what was then the Buffalo–Cleveland road, now marooned in Midtown with several acres of gardens around it.
places.k: Wednesday and Sunday afternoons only, and the tour is given by volunteers who know an enormous amount.

places.w: A genuinely enormous independent bookshop on Larchmere — room after room of towering wooden stacks, a serious antiquarian section, and a vaulted room called the Sanctuary for first editions. Open seven days.

Boardwalk trails through marsh and woodland inside the city limits, on land saved from a proposed freeway by a residents' campaign in the 1960s — one of the first environmental fights of its kind in America. Free, and largely accessible.
places.k: Closed Monday.

places.w: One of the best repertory cinemas in the country, inside the art institute — restorations, world cinema, and films that will not screen anywhere else within three hundred miles.
places.k: Check the calendar; screenings are scheduled, not continuous. Entrance is down the side of the building.

places.n: The RainForest, Cleveland Metroparks Zoo — CLOSED
places.w: A two-storey simulated Amazon under glass, with an open aviary you walk through, a pool where it rains on a schedule, and a fog that rolls off the water. Included with zoo admission; parking is free.

pv.ss: clevelandmetroparks.com / Fox8 / WKYC — RainForest closed to public for the $60M Primate/Tropical Forest rebuild

places.w: A living-history village inside the national park — working blacksmith, glassblower and potter, period buildings moved here from across the Western Reserve, and costumed interpreters at weekends in season.
places.k: Wednesday to Sunday, seasonal. Pairs naturally with Brandywine Falls and the scenic railroad.

places.n: @neorsd — not a place, but on the list
places.ad: Northeast Ohio Regional Sewer District, 3900 Euclid Ave
places.w: The only entry on News 5's hidden-gems list that is not a physical location. The Northeast Ohio Regional Sewer District's social account was, in their assessment, the best in Cleveland — a delight that transcends the list's otherwise earthly bounds. Pinned to their headquarters so nothing is missing, but there is nothing to visit.
places.k: Do not drive here. Follow the account instead.

places.w: A Cleveland icon from April 1985 that covered 3.1 million miles over 37 years. It shut down permanently in May 2022. Listed here for completeness — Lake View Cemetery still runs its own trolley tours.
places.k: Do not plan around this one. It no longer runs.

places.w: The largest performing-arts and arts-education center on Cleveland's West Shore — a nonprofit founded in 1931 (as Lakewood Little Theatre) that entertains and educates 65,000+ people a year across two stages on a 3.5-acre Detroit Ave campus. Professional theater, galleries, and classes; documented by the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History and listed by TourismOhio.
s: Encyclopedia of Cleveland History (CWRU) — Lakewood Little Theatre / Beck Center (est. 1931)
Ohio.org — Beck Center for the Arts, Lakewood

places.n: Rocky River Reservation & Fort Hill Stairs
places.w: A Cleveland Metroparks jewel of the Emerald Necklace winding along the Rocky River — over five miles of trails to river's edge, wetlands, ponds and ancient Native American earthworks, plus the Fort Hill Stairs (155 steps rising 90 ft to a bluff-top view). The Rocky River Nature Center displays the prehistoric fish Dunkleosteus and the kid-favorite HideAway Hollow oak.
s: Cleveland Metroparks — Rocky River Reservation & Nature Center; Fort Hill Stairs
Cleveland Scene — Rocky River Nature Center, Western Suburbs

places.ad: Lake Rd at Wolf Rd, Bay Village, OH 44140
places.w: A ~100-acre Cleveland Metroparks lakefront reservation in Bay Village with a swimming beach on Lake Erie, three miles of trails through beach-forest-meadow habitats, and the landmark 1927 Huntington water tower with a play space and snack spot. Home to two Metroparks affiliates (Lake Erie Nature & Science Center and BAYarts).
s: OhioDNR / Ohio.org — Huntington Reservation, Lake Erie Birding Trail

places.w: One of the oldest municipally owned arts parks in the U.S., conceived in 1938 by Heights drama teacher Dr. Dina Rees Evans and Mayor Frank C. Cain — the covered 2,782-seat Evans Amphitheater, the Alma Theater, the Feinberg gallery, and the July Cain Park Arts Festival, a nationally top-rated juried outdoor art fair. Entrances at Lee Rd and Superior Park Dr.
s: cleveland.com — Cain Park Arts Festival, top-rated outdoor arts festival

places.w: Cleveland's premier arthouse cinema and the anchor of the Cedar Lee district — open since 1925 and now a six-screen Cleveland Cinemas house for indie, foreign and documentary films, famous for its monthly midnight 'Rocky Horror Picture Show.'
s: Cleveland Scene — Cedar Lee Theatre, indie/foreign arthouse (Rocky Horror midnight)
cleveland.com — Cedar Lee, historic Cleveland Heights cinema (1925)

places.w: Vietnamese-owned and family-run in Asiatown, and by consensus the best phở in the city. The bone broth simmers 24 hours from a recipe passed down through the family; the owner is known to throw out an entire vat that doesn't meet standard. Fourteen versions of phở, plus bánh mì, bún thịt nướng, summer rolls and proper Vietnamese coffee.
places.k: Enter through Golden Plaza, a nondescript mini-mall with free parking. Closed Monday. Do not confuse it with Number One Pho two doors down — people mix them up constantly.

places.w: Two doors from Superior Phở and a genuine rival. Cleveland Magazine singles out the wider Vietnamese menu — vermicelli bowls, broken rice, and chả trứng, the steamed egg cake that comes with the rice plates and that you will not find elsewhere in town.
places.k: Closed Wednesday. Fish sauce wings are the sleeper order.

places.w: Vietnamese, family-run, and in the same room since 1984 — the oldest Vietnamese restaurant in Cleveland. The signature is the #21 cinnamon rare beef phở; regulars also come for the vermicelli with grilled pork, the crêpes (bánh xèo) and the homemade chilli oil.
places.k: Reviews from 2025 mention the family planning to close. Call before you make a trip — and if it is open, go.

pv.ss: cleveland.com 'closing permanently' + Cleveland Scene — last day Sun Sep 12 after 37 years; Yelp CLOSED May 2026

places.w: A counter and a few tables at the back of a grocery, inside a mall. Cleveland Scene sends people here for bún bò Huế — the spicy Huế beef noodle soup — and for shrimp wonton noodle soup loaded with pork dumplings and egg noodles. There's a bun bakery attached.
places.k: Not a restaurant in any conventional sense. Go in, walk to the back, order at the counter.

places.w: The only Singaporean kitchen I can find in Cleveland, and it passes the test. Confirmed on the menu: chai tow kway (white carrot cake, which they will make Singapore-spicy if you ask), curry laksa, roti, and pork bao — Hokkien and Teochew dishes cooked as dishes, not as an idea of Singapore. Three house chilli oils. A diner who lived in Singapore ten years went specifically to test it and stayed.
places.k:
Closed Sunday and Monday; dinner-only most nights (4:30–9), Friday from noon, Saturday 12–3 then 4:30–8:30. Small room — call ahead.

Honest caveat: I could not confirm char kway teow or Hainanese chicken rice on the current menu, and the menu is short and rotates. Ask when you call. What I can confirm is that there is no “Singapore noodles” nonsense here.

places.w: The Infatuation's line on it: the owner set out to serve the food her mother cooks at home, and her mother works in the kitchen. Bangkok-style rather than Americanised. Go for the green papaya salad, the potstickers and the lemongrass barbecued chicken on a stick.
places.k: Closed Tuesday, dinner only from 4pm. Tiny room — not a group dinner. Two doors from Dang Good, so you can scout both.

places.w: Reputed to be the spiciest Thai kitchen in Cleveland, and it does not soften things for the room. Som tam, tom yum and a duck dish people come back for.
places.k: Closed Monday. Small and cosy; the Buddha room seats about twenty.

places.w: Filipino, and the highest-rated Asian restaurant in the Cleveland area by diner score. Lechon pork belly, tofu sisig, pancit bihon, ginataang, halo-halo. Filipino reviewers write about walking in and feeling homesick — which is the review that matters.
places.k: Closed Monday. Worth the twenty-minute drive south.

places.n: Li Wah — Cantonese dim sum carts
places.w: Cantonese. Freshwater calls it the best dim sum in Cleveland and it is still the only place running proper steel carts at weekend lunch — har gow, siu mai, chicken feet, roast duck, rice rolls, circling the room. Hundreds of people pack it on Saturday and Sunday.
places.k: Carts run weekend lunch only; come before 1pm or you get the menu instead. Some off-cart dishes draw mixed reviews — stick to dim sum and roast meats.

places.w: Cantonese / Hong Kong-style. Freshwater rates it the best Chinese restaurant in Asiatown and says some would extend that to all of Northeast Ohio. Roast duck and char siu hanging in the window, chive pot stickers, shrimp wonton noodle soup, three-flavour dumpling soup, salt-baked shrimp, soy sauce chicken, beef chow fun. Full-colour photos of nearly every dish cover three of the four walls.
places.k: Closed Tuesday. Cash-friendly, cheap, and not remotely fancy.

places.w: Cantonese. The other dim sum house, and Cleveland Magazine's pick for late night — open past midnight, until 2am Friday and Saturday. Har gow and shrimp rice rolls get named repeatedly.
places.k: Under new ownership and remodelled; reviews since are mixed on the wider menu but consistent on the dim sum.

places.w: Cantonese seafood, despite the Thai name — thirty years in, live tanks, Hong Kong-style dishes, whole steamed fish, pork belly with preserved vegetable. Diners who know Cantonese cooking single out the fried clams for being fried properly.
places.k: Big room, ample parking, huge portions. The Thai-sounding dishes are not the reason to come.

places.w: Sichuan. Cleveland Magazine calls it a favourite standby of Cleveland chefs. Cumin lamb skewers, scallion pancakes, and a spice level that is not adjusted for the room — mind the traditional dishes.

Lebanese-Palestinian, directly across from West Side Market, and the reason a lot of market regulars skip the market food stalls. Shawarma, kafta, hummus, and a garlic sauce people write paragraphs about.
places.k: Lunch only — closes at 3pm most days, 4pm Saturday, closed Sunday.

places.w: Turkish, and the real thing — İskender kebab, döner carved from actual stacked meat rather than the processed gyro cone, red lentil soup, rakı, and baklava. Reviewers who have just come back from Turkey rate it against Turkey.
places.k:
Closed Monday.

On Persian specifically: I searched and could not find a Persian restaurant in Cleveland with the kind of rave or viral reputation you asked for. Rather than pad the list with something mediocre, I'm telling you it isn't there. Anatolia is the closest strong option in the region.

places.w: Colombian-Venezuelan, and the arepa place Cleveland actually argues about — 3,300 reviews at 4.6. Arepas, cachapas, empanadas, birria arepa, and mojitos that people order first. Named repeatedly in Infatuation and Yelp's Venezuelan rankings.
places.k: Waits get long and they do not shorten. Five minutes from Dang Good on the same road.

pv.ss: Yelp CLOSED banner; WKYC/Crain's/westlifenews/hoodline closing stories; own Facebook farewell post

places.w: Guatemalan and Salvadoran, family-run, and the pupusas are what people come back for — plus the black beans, which several reviewers call the best in Cleveland. Everything is cooked to order, so it takes time.
places.k: Closed Monday. Ten minutes from the Buckland witchcraft museum.

places.w: Modern Mexican, luchador decor, and a guacamole list — the smoked trout and bacon version is the one. Barbacoa for two, and fried ice cream to finish. A Cleveland fixture for close to twenty years.
places.k: Closed Sunday. Reserve or expect an hour at the bar.

places.w: Eastern European, run by three sisters across several generations of the same family. Wiener schnitzel, cevapi, stuffed cabbage, city chicken, dumplings and gravy, and homemade strudel. Cheap, slow, and exactly what people mourn now that Sokolowski's is gone.
places.k: Closed Sunday. Service is unhurried by design.

places.w: Central and Eastern European deli technique crossed with koji fermentation — the Japanese fungus used to fast-forward curing, which gives their pastrami a salt-sweet umami layer nothing else in the city has. Menu changes daily and is announced on Instagram. James Beard-recognised.
places.k: Hours have contracted sharply — recent listings show Saturday only. Check Instagram the morning you plan to go.

places.w: Bourdain ate here. He opened the 2007 No Reservations Cleveland episode with a three-way — spaghetti, cinnamon-spiced chili, shredded cheddar — explicitly to needle his Cleveland-native guide Michael Ruhlman, since Skyline is a Cincinnati thing. Clevelanders were furious. That is exactly why it's here.
places.k: Greek-Macedonian-style chili, sweet and cinnamon-forward. Not what you think chili is. Order a four-way with onions.

pv.ss: Yelp CLOSED banner; Skyline official locations page 'CLOSED'; Cleveland Jewish News & Cleveland Scene closing stories

places.w: The corned beef sandwich Cleveland argues about — absurdly overstacked, and a fixture of national food TV for decades. Also the best pastrami on toasted rye in the city, by a number of accounts.
places.k: Monday to Friday, 7am–2:30pm. Closed both weekend days. Go early; the queue is real. Roughly $25 a sandwich now.

places.n: Melt Bar and Grilled — the original — CLOSED
places.w: The first Melt, and a repeat feature on national food television for the sheer scale of the grilled cheese. The Lake Erie Monster and the Dude Abides are the classics. Unusually good vegan menu for a place built on cheese.

pv.ss: Yelp CLOSED banner; WKYC, Ideastream, Cleveland Magazine, Cleveland19 closing stories

places.w: Roughly fifty toppings on a tick-sheet — which alone would not earn a listing. What does is the programming: the same room books punk bands, polka nights, and members of the Cleveland Orchestra playing chamber music to a bar crowd.
places.k: Half-price happy hour is how to explore the topping list without regret. Open late.

places.w: A hot dog cart that went properly viral on local social media and holds a 4.8 across hundreds of reviews. Twelve-inch build-your-own, homemade chili, and a flaming-hot-Cheeto elote dog that has no business working and does.
places.k: Thursday to Saturday, roughly midday to 3–4pm, and they sell out. This is a cart, not a restaurant.

places.w: Michael Symon's attempt at a Cleveland barbecue idiom — Eastern European spicing, kielbasa alongside the brisket, pickles from Tony Packo's, and a platter literally called This Is Cleveland. The beef rib is the order.
places.k: Closed Monday.

places.w: The Infatuation's framing is “Midwest nice” — fancied-up 1990s Ohio food. The signature is a White Castle-inspired burger box: one enormous smashburger that tears into four sliders with smoked cheddar and pickles marinated in Kool-Aid. Best pierogi several reviewers say they have eaten.
places.k: Closed Monday. Book the kitchen counter if there are three or fewer of you.

places.ad: 3441 Tuttle Rd, Van Aken Market, Shaker Heights
places.w: Poutine and sausage, and an elote corndog. Uneven by report — the fries and the jalapeño popper slider are the consistent things.

Made on site in a restored 1920s cinema, with a glass wall so you watch the production floor while you eat. Lavender honey and the Cleveland brownie sundae are the ones people name. Two minutes from West Side Market.
A full 1920s-style soda fountain rebuilt from scratch — marble counter, hand-pumped syrups, enormous sundaes, and a candy counter. The root beer float is the order.
places.k: Queues badly at weekends and service can lag. Free parking behind the arcade.

pv.ss: Yelp CLOSED banner; own Facebook farewell post; Fox8, WKYC, Cleveland Jewish News, Cleveland Scene closing stories

places.w: A century-old Italian bakery and the anchor of Little Italy. Cannoli, sfogliatelle, lady locks, Linzer cookies, plus savoury Stromboli and artichoke pizza. Take a number or you will get cut in line.

Directly across from Presti's, and the rivalry is the point — go to both and pick a side. Corbo's does not pre-fill its cannoli shells, and is the place for cassata cake and sfogliatelle. Closed Monday.
Taiwanese bakery and bubble tea, and where the Infatuation tells you to get a coconut cream bun after phở. Buns sweet and savoury, egg tarts, and the best boba in the city by most local accounts.
places.k: Closed Tuesday.

places.w: Old Brooklyn institution since 1974, honey-sweetened, and the flavour Clevelanders grew up on. Orange blossom is the signature.
A Cleveland chocolate house since 1935, with a table-service ice cream parlour attached — pretzels come free with your sundae, for dipping in their hot fudge. Same road as Dang Good.

A brewery inside a converted church, disco ball included, in Lakewood's historic Birdtown — the Czech and Slovak workers' district built around the old Union Rolling Mill, where the streets are named after birds. Pizza and wings are the order.

Indoor mini golf over two floors, each with its own bar and its own atmosphere — the club course upstairs, the lounge course in the basement. Every hole has somewhere to rest a drink. Eight minutes from Dang Good.
places.k: Closed Monday. Around $13 for nine holes, $20 for eighteen.

places.w: Organic, largely vegetarian and entirely made in house — coffee, pizza, salads, and live jazz some evenings. Composts everything. The best room on this side of town to sit in for two hours with nobody minding.

Bourdain's favourite stop in Cleveland — chicken paprikash, stuffed cabbage, head cheese and boiled pig's head, served cafeteria-style. “This might be the greatest establishment ever,” he said. A James Beard America's Classic. It closed after 100 years in the same family. Listed so you know it is gone rather than wondering.
places.k: Closed permanently. Marie's on St Clair is the closest living equivalent.

places.w: Where Bourdain ate a Polish Boy — kielbasa, fries, coleslaw and barbecue sauce in one bun, Cleveland's own invention. Also closed. The Polish Boy lives on at Happy Dog, Banter and most Cleveland barbecue counters.
places.k: Closed permanently.

places.w: A Barberton Serbian-fried-chicken mainstay since 1950 — crisp lard-fried quarters with the signature hot rice, slaw and fries; the childhood go-to for many locals. About 35 min south.

Norton's country roadhouse for Barberton-style chicken — juicy lard-fried birds with an especially craveable crust, the traditional hot sauce and sides, in a wood-paneled room regulars swear edges out the rest. About 40 min south.

A restored 1938 Tremont corner bar and Cleveland landmark whose Friday Lake Erie yellow-perch fry draws a line out the door — lager, duckpin-era charm and one of the city's great fish sandwiches. Come early.
A west-suburban tavern that fries fresh Lake Erie yellow perch every Friday year-round (not just Lent) — the go-to for locals who take their perch seriously. About 20 min west.
A tiny, well-worn Lakewood neighborhood pub whose Lenten Friday fish and Lake Erie perch fries are a west-side ritual — cash-friendly, unpretentious, packed. About 15 min west.

Sam McNulty's Ohio City anchor brewery (2011), right across from the West Side Market — a 320-seat brewpub with a 3,000-sq-ft American beer garden, three fireplaces, and a rooftop patio, plus a full production brewhouse. A cornerstone of Ohio City's Brewing District and a regular on Cleveland Magazine's best-breweries guide.
s: Cleveland's 28 Best Breweries: Market Garden Brewery
Cleveland Scene — Ohio City Brewing District / best breweries
